title: Should We Combine Our Data?Algorithms and Limits for Privately Assessing Data Sharing

paper.title: Should We Combine Our Data? Algorithms and Limits for Privately Assessing Data Sharing
paper.abstract: Abstract In this paper, we study when two parties should pool their data to train a machine learning model. Two agents, Alice and Bob, each hold a sensitive labeled dataset and want to train a classifier from a given hypothesis class ℋ \mathcal{H} . Even when each party’s dataset can be perfectly classified on its own, the two parties may follow conflicting labeling standards or have selection biases that affect their features and label sets, such that no single classifier in ℋ \mathcal{H} fits their combined data. Before committing to data sharing, Alice and Bob therefore want to test whether a single classifier in ℋ \mathcal{H} can jointly fit both datasets—without revealing their individual data points to one another. We formalize this problem from a learning-theoretic viewpoint via opt ℋ \operatorname{opt}_{\mathcal{H}} , the minimum number of mistakes made by any hypothesis in ℋ \mathcal{H} on their pooled data. Through interactive communication, the agents must distinguish opt ℋ = 0 \operatorname{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}=0 (compatible datasets) from opt ℋ ≥ t \operatorname{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}\geq t (conflicting datasets) under pure ε \varepsilon -two-party differential privacy. A trusted curator could do this with t = O ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) t=O(1/\varepsilon) , and we ask how small t t can be without one. For thresholds on the real line over a domain of size m m , we show that the optimal t t is Θ ~ ​ ( log ⁡ log ⁡ m / ε ) \tilde{\Theta}(\log\log m/\varepsilon) , exponentially smaller than the Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ m / ε ) \Theta(\log m/\varepsilon) samples needed to privately learn thresholds, even with a curator. For halfspaces in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , the dependence on m m jumps to log ⁡ ( m ) \log(m) : we give a protocol with t = O ~ ​ ( d 3 ​ log ⁡ m / ε ) t=\tilde{O}(d^{3}\log m/\varepsilon) and show that some domains require t = Ω ⁡ ( d ​ log ⁡ ( m / d ) / ε ) t=\Omega(d\log(m/d)/\varepsilon) .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Institutions often hold complementary datasets that capture different aspects of the same downstream learning task. For example, a breast screening clinic may hold primarily negative cases, while a specialized diagnostic center may hold a much higher proportion of confirmed cancer cases [ LASLBKHOTRM17 , SAMHBORLTKLB17 ] . Similarly, organizations trying to detect cybersecurity incidents frequently share data to provide a comprehensive view of the cybersecurity landscape, as attackers may target different organizations with different exploits at different times [ CH23 ] . In such settings, pooling data may enable institutions to learn a useful classifier that no entity could learn on its own. Indeed, this potential was highlighted and analyzed in early theoretical works on distributed machine learning [ BBFM12 ] . Realizing the potential benefit of collaboration, however, often requires institutions to commit resources upfront through legal agreements, financial compensation, governance approvals, and dedicated infrastructure. Before incurring these costs, institutions need to assess the utility of combining their datasets: will pooling improve model accuracy or other downstream metrics enough to justify the collaboration? Yet this assessment depends on joint properties of the datasets, generally hidden from each institution’s local view. Institutions face a circular dilemma: they must judge whether collaboration is worthwhile before committing, yet doing so may require the very data sharing whose value they seek to assess. Privacy requirements further complicate this dilemma. Hospitals, for example, must protect sensitive patient records even when sharing them would help evaluate a collaboration. Institutions may also hesitate to disclose valuable data to a prospective partner who could use them independently and decline to collaborate. When no trusted third party is available, each party must therefore assess whether collaboration is promising while limiting what it reveals about its data. This tension between the need to preserve data privacy while enabling agents to assess the utility of collaboration motivates the main conceptual question of this paper: How can agents estimate whether it is beneficial to combine their datasets while preserving the privacy of individual records? What algorithms can achieve this goal, and what are their fundamental limits?

sections.heading: 1.1 How to Assess the Benefits of Data Sharing?
sections.text: In this section, we propose a learning-theoretic notion that agents can use to assess the value of data sharing and provide two real-world scenarios in which it can inform the decision to collaborate. Our focus throughout the paper is on binary classification on a data space (or feature space) 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ d \mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} of size m m for some d ≥ 1 d\geq 1 and a fixed publicly known hypothesis class ℋ ⊆ { ± 1 } 𝒳 \mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{\mathcal{X}} . We consider a setting with two agents, Alice ( A A ) and Bob ( B B ) who respecitvely hold a labeled dataset S A , S B ∈ ( 𝒳 × { ± 1 } ) n S_{A},S_{B}\in(\mathcal{X}\times\{\pm 1\})^{n} of size n ∈ ℕ n\in\mathbb{N} . We focus on a basic question that arises before joint training: can a single classifier in a given hypothesis class explain both parties’ data? We formalize this question using their joint empirical loss defined as opt ℋ ( S A , S B ) := min h ∈ ℋ ∑ U ∈ { A , B } ∑ ( x , y ) ∈ S U 𝟏 { h ( x ) ≠ y } . \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B}):=\newmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{U\in\{A,B\}}\sum_{(x,y)\in S_{U}}\mathbf{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{h(x)\neq y}}\right\}. (1) We use opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B}) , the number of mistakes made on the pooled data by the best classifier in ℋ \mathcal{H} , to assess the value of combining the data. It is zero when one hypothesis explains both datasets, and large when every hypothesis in ℋ \mathcal{H} makes many mistakes on their union. A large joint loss may indicate conflicting labeling practices, selection biases causing missing features and labels, or that the hypothesis class is not complex enough to fit the combined data. We therefore focus on distinguishing between the following: opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) = 0 \displaystyle\mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})=0 opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) ≥ t \displaystyle\mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})\geq t (2) for some t > 0 t>0 . When opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) = 0 \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})=0 , Alice and Bob agree to collaborate. When opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) ≥ t \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})\geq t , Alice and Bob must reassess 1 1 1 This could take the form of Alice and Bob realizing they do not have the expertise or computing power to fit a good model, in which case they refuse to collaborate; or, this could mean that Alice and Bob need to reconcile their labeling practices, jointly rectify their selection biases to account for missingness, potentially re-label data, or choose a more complex hypothesis class. . Finally, if 0 < opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) < t 0<\mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})<t , we make no claims, as is standard in distribution testing. We now present two examples that further motivate the property-testing problem in ( 2 ). Example 1 (Learning from disparate label sets) . Suppose Alice is a screening clinician and Bob is a diagnostician. They want to develop a classifier to determine whether a patient in a target population should be referred for further diagnostic testing. Their datasets reflect different stages of care: Alice’s screening dataset S A S_{A} mainly contains records of patients who were not referred, whereas Bob’s diagnostic dataset S B S_{B} contains only records of patients who were referred and received more thorough testing [ GBRRDJM11 ] . Since the records contain sensitive patient information, neither agent is willing to disclose individual records to assess a possible collaboration, and no trusted third party is available. To isolate this selection bias, suppose Alice’s labels are all − 1 -1 , and Bob’s are all + 1 +1 . Then, neither can train a useful model alone; they must assess opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B}) to determine whether they can train a low-error model on their joint data. Example 2 (Identifying conflicting labeling practices) . Now suppose Alice has labeled spam and non-spam emails in her dataset. However, her data may be limited or imbalanced, so she wants to augment it with Bob’s curated, labeled email dataset. The challenge is that Bob may have a different view of what constitutes spam, so his labels could conflict with Alice’s data [ KCG24 ] . For example, Alice may label unsolicited promotional emails as spam, while Bob uses that label for fraudulent or malicious messages. Before joint training, Alice wants to know whether a single classifier can achieve a sufficiently low test error under both labeling policies. To isolate conflicting labeling practices, suppose the agents encounter the same distribution of emails but may assign different labels to the same email. In this case, opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) = 0 \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})=0 indicates that, under the hypothesis class H H , Alice’s and Bob’s labeling practices are compatible, implying a collaboration may be worthwhile. On the other end, opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) ≥ t \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})\geq t points to differing labeling practices. Remark 1.1 (From in-sample to in-population error) . Note that our insights extend beyond the in-sample case and hold when considering generalization error over the underlying population distributions. We provide more details using standard arguments in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 1.2 Problem Formalization
sections.text:
In this section, we formalize our problem and state our main technical question. We first consider the disjoint-label setting as in Example 1 , where Alice holds only negatively labeled examples, and Bob holds only positively labeled ones. Since the labels are fixed by the party holding each record, we suppress them and write S A , S B ∈ 𝒳 n S_{A},\ S_{B}\in\mathcal{X}^{n} . This setting isolates the joint aspect of the problem: when ℋ \mathcal{H} contains the constant predictors, each local dataset is perfectly realizable, but their union need not be. Thus, the local optimal errors alone do not determine whether a common classifier can explain both datasets. For our algorithms, we later show that they extend to datasets with arbitrary label mixtures (see Corollaries 3.13 and 4.8 ). They seek a private assessment algorithm that rejects with high probability when every classifier in ℋ \mathcal{H} makes at least t t mistakes on the pooled data, i.e., opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) ≥ t \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})\geq t . We call this requirement soundness . However, a trivial algorithm that always rejects also satisfies soundness. We therefore also require the algorithm to accept with high probability when the pooled data are jointly realizable, i.e., opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) = 0 \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})=0 , a requirement we call completeness . Finally, to protect the privacy of individual records throughout the interaction, we use differential privacy [ DMNS06 ] in its two-party form [ BNO08 , MMPRTV10 ] , which requires each agent’s view to be differentially private with respect to the other agent’s dataset (see Definition 2.1 ). Fix a data space 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , a hypothesis class ℋ ⊆ { ± 1 } 𝒳 \mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{\mathcal{X}} , a dataset size n ∈ ℕ n\in\mathbb{N} , a privacy parameter ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 , and t ∈ [ 2 ​ n ] t\in[2n] . Completeness. For every S A , S B ∈ 𝒳 n S_{A},S_{B}\in\mathcal{X}^{n} , s.t. opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) = 0 \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})=0 , we have Pr [ Π ( S A , S B ) = 𝖬𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁 ] ≥ 0.9 . \Pr\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\Pi(S_{A},S_{B})=\mathsf{Match}}}ight]\geq 0.9. The probabilities are over the protocol’s private and public randomness. We seek the smallest achievable resolution t t , since smaller values let agents enforce stricter error tolerances. Without privacy constraints, the agents can exchange their datasets and compute opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B}) exactly, achieving t = 1 t=1 , the best possible resolution. A trusted curator could also ensure differential privacy by releasing opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) + Lap ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})+\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon) , since the joint loss has sensitivity one. This gives a tester with resolution t central = O ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) t_{	ext{central}}=O(1/\varepsilon) , independent of the dimension and hypothesis class. However, we require information-theoretic two-party differential privacy without a trusted curator. This motivates the main technical question that our paper seeks to answer: For fixed ℋ \mathcal{H} and ε \varepsilon , what is the smallest resolution t t that an ε \varepsilon -DP private tester can guarantee?

sections.heading: 1.3 Our Results
sections.text: We answer the above technical question for two fundamental classes of hypotheses: thresholds on the real line and half-spaces in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} . For each class, we establish both upper and lower bounds on the optimal resolution t t of any ε \varepsilon -private tester (summarized in Table 1 ). Notably, our main interactive protocols achieve a resolution t t that is completely independent of the dataset size n n , and all of our upper bounds extend immediately from the disjoint-label setting to arbitrary mixed-label datasets (see Corollaries 3.13 and 4.8 ).

sections.heading: 1.4 Technical Overview
sections.text: In this section, we outline the main ideas behind our lower bounds and private testing algorithms. We first explain in Section 1.4.1 the idea behind our lower bound, which is based on the connection between opt ℋ \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}} and error-correcting codes. We then describe in Section 1.4.2 , our threshold algorithm which uses private binary search over prefix lengths to compare two ordered blocks of data. Finally, in Section 1.4.3 , we explain the ideas behind our algorithm for halfspaces, which is based on the cutting-plane method in the dual space, i.e., classifier space.

sections.heading: 1.4.1 Lower Bounds: Coding Against Erasures
sections.text: Our lower bounds use the connection between information complexity and DP [ MMPRTV10 ] . We consider a communication problem in which Alice and Bob receive secrets v A , v B ∈ 𝒱 v_{A},v_{B}\in\mathcal{V} in a finite domain 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , and exchange messages to compute a binary function F : 𝒱 × 𝒱 → { 0 , 1 } F:\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{V}\to\{0,1\} . For a protocol computing F F on inputs ( V A , V B ) ∼ μ (V_{A},V_{B})\sim\mu , let Π \Pi denote its public transcript, including public randomness, exchanged messages, and final output. The protocol’s internal information cost is defined as IC μ ⁡ ( Π , F ) := I ⁡ ( V A ; Π ∣ V B ) + I ⁡ ( V B ; Π ∣ V A ) \operatorname{IC}_{\mu}(\Pi,F):=I(V_{A};\Pi\mid V_{B})+I(V_{B};\Pi\mid V_{A}) . Intuitively, it measures what the transcript reveals about each input, given the other. To force a private tester to incur a large information cost, we choose F F and μ \mu such that every protocol Π \Pi computing F F with bounded error has large IC μ ⁡ ( Π , F ) \operatorname{IC}_{\mu}(\Pi,F) . To relate the communication problem to our problem, we construct local encoders E A , E B : 𝒱 → 𝒳 n E_{A},E_{B}:\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{X}^{n} , producing datasets S A = E A ​ ( v A ) S_{A}=E_{A}(v_{A}) and S B = E B ​ ( v B ) S_{B}=E_{B}(v_{B}) that satisfy F ⁡ ( v A , v B ) = 0 ⟹ opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) = 0 , and F ⁡ ( v A , v B ) = 1 ⟹ opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) ≥ t . \displaystyle F(v_{A},v_{B})=0\implies\mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})=0,\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(v_{A},v_{B})=1\implies\mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})\geq t. Running a private tester with resolution t t on these datasets therefore yields a bounded-error protocol Π \Pi for F F . To capture the sensitivity of the encoders to the secrets, we define the encoding diameters Δ U ​ ( n , t ) := max v , v ′ ∈ 𝒱 d ham ​ ( E U ​ ( v ) , E U ​ ( v ′ ) ) \Delta_{U}(n,t):=\newmax_{v,v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}}\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{ham}}(E_{U}(v),E_{U}(v^{\prime})) for U ∈ { A , B } U\in\{A,B\} , and write Δ = Δ ⁡ ( n , t ) := Δ A ​ ( n , t ) + Δ B ​ ( n , t ) \Delta=\Delta(n,t):=\Delta_{A}(n,t)+\Delta_{B}(n,t) . The delicacy is that we need to design an encoding function that relates the encoding diameters to n , t n,t . Then, we can invoke existing results [ MMPRTV10 ] (also see Lemma 2.2 ) that show that IC μ ⁡ ( Π , F ) ≤ O ⁡ ( ε ​ Δ ) \operatorname{IC}_{\mu}(\Pi,F)\leq O(\varepsilon\Delta) . Comparing this upper bound with the information required to compute F F forces Δ \Delta to be large. Our encoders upper-bound Δ \Delta in terms of the loss gap t t , turning this requirement into a lower bound on t t . To design encoders for Alice and Bob, we link joint empirical loss to robustness against record erasures. For any hypothesis class ℋ \mathcal{H} , opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B}) equals the minimum number of records that must be removed from the pooled data to make it realizable. Thus, ensuring opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) ≥ t \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})\geq t requires the pooled data to remain non-realizable after removing any set of fewer than t t records. This suggests using error-correcting codes to make non-realizability robust to erasures while keeping the encoding diameter small. Repetition suffices for thresholds, while our halfspace construction uses an expander code. For thresholds on a domain 𝒳 ⊂ ℝ \mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R} of size m m , Alice and Bob hold inputs v A , v B ∈ 𝒱 = 𝒳 v_{A},v_{B}\in\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{X} . We use the Greater-Than predicate F ( v A , v B ) = 𝟏 { v A ≥ v B } F(v_{A},v_{B})=\mathbf{1}\{v_{A}\geq v_{B}\} . Alice creates t t copies of ( v A , − 1 ) (v_{A},-1) , and Bob creates t t copies of ( v B , + 1 ) (v_{B},+1) . The pooled data are realizable when v A < v B v_{A}<v_{B} , whereas every threshold misclassifies an entire block when v A ≥ v B v_{A}\geq v_{B} . This gives a loss gap of t t with encoding diameter Δ = O ⁡ ( t ) \Delta=O(t) . Since Greater-Than has information complexity Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ log ⁡ m ) \Omega(\log\log m) under a suitable input distribution [ BW11 ] , we use prior results connecting DP to information complexity [ MMPRTV10 ] ( Lemma 2.2 ) to compare this lower bound with an O ⁡ ( ε ​ t ) O(\varepsilon t) privacy bound, yielding t = Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ log ⁡ ( m ) / ε ) t=\Omega(\log\log(m)/\varepsilon) . For halfspaces , Alice and Bob hold vectors v A , v B ∈ 𝒱 = 𝔽 q k v_{A},v_{B}\in\mathcal{V}=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k} , where k = Θ ⁡ ( d ) k=\Theta(d) and q q is a power of two. Our encoders map these inputs to labeled data points in a public feature domain 𝒳 ⊂ ℝ d \mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} of size m m . We use the trace inner-product predicate F ⁡ ( v A , v B ) = Tr 𝔽 q / 𝔽 2 ⁡ ( ∑ i = 1 k v A , i ​ v B , i ) F(v_{A},v_{B})=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}/\mathbb{F}_{2}}(\sum_{i=1}^{k}v_{A,i}v_{B,i}) , whose information complexity is Ω ⁡ ( k ​ log ⁡ q ) \Omega(k\log q) ( Lemma B.6 ). To construct the datasets, we view halfspace consistency as a linear feasibility problem, with classifier parameters as variables and one constraint per labeled record. We use this correspondence in reverse, building an LP and converting its constraints into records. For each i ∈ [ k ] i\in[k] , Alice supplies one input-dependent, or private , constraint fixing the LP representation of v A , i v_{A,i} , and Bob does the same for v B , i v_{B,i} . The input-independent public constraints force an output variable z z to equal F ⁡ ( v A , v B ) F(v_{A},v_{B}) once the private constraints fix the inputs. They also require z = 0 z=0 , making the LP feasible iff F ⁡ ( v A , v B ) = 0 F(v_{A},v_{B})=0 . To obtain a loss gap of t t , we could repeat every constraint t t times, as for thresholds. However, the resulting diameter Δ = O ⁡ ( k ​ t ) \Delta=O(kt) cancels the dimension factor in the information comparison k ​ log ⁡ q ≲ ε ​ k ​ t k\log q\lesssim\varepsilon kt (see Section 4.1.1 ). We instead encode v A v_{A} and v B v_{B} using an expander code with Θ ⁡ ( k ) \Theta(k) symbols and constant-size checks [ FWK05 , FMSSW07 ] . Private constraints fix the codeword symbols, while public constraints enforce the code checks. Our key step shows that, with public constraints enforced, fewer than D = Θ ⁡ ( d ) D=\Theta(d) private deletions cannot change the codewords, even through fractional LP solutions. Indeed, unique-neighbor expansion gives any nonempty set of fewer than D D deviating symbols a check touching exactly one of them; the unchanged symbols force it back to its original value. Thus, repeating each private constraint ⌈ t / D ⌉ \lceil t/D\rceil times and each public constraint t t times prevents fewer than t t record deletions from restoring realizability when F ⁡ ( v A , v B ) = 1 F(v_{A},v_{B})=1 . Only private copies affect the diameter, giving Δ = O ⁡ ( d ⁡ ⌈ t / D ⌉ ) = O ⁡ ( t + d ) \Delta=O(d\lceil t/D\rceil)=O(t+d) . Finally, we represent field elements as polygon vertices in ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} ; restricting each symbol to this polygon lets one supporting inequality fix its value. Together with sparse checks, this keeps the dimension O ⁡ ( d ) O(d) and the universe size O ⁡ ( d ​ q O ⁡ ( 1 ) ) O(dq^{O(1)}) . Choosing q = ( m / d ) Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) q=(m/d)^{\Theta(1)} and applying the information bound yields t = Ω ⁡ ( d ​ log ⁡ ( m / d ) / ε ) t=\Omega(d\log(m/d)/\varepsilon) under the parameter conditions of Theorem 4.1 .

sections.heading: 1.4.2 Algorithm for Thresholds: A Robust and Private Greater-Than Protocol
sections.text: Figure 2 : Reduction to witness blocks for thresholds with disjoint supports. Alice retains her largest k = ⌊ t / 2 ⌋ k=\lfloor t/2\rfloor records, and Bob retains his smallest k k records. Solid points are retained and used by our algorithm; faded points are discarded and never be used by our algorithm. In 𝖬𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁 \mathsf{Match} , Alice’s retained block lies entirely below Bob’s; in 𝖥𝖺𝗋 \mathsf{Far} , their order is reversed. The illustration uses n = 8 n=8 , t = 6 t=6 , and k = 3 k=3 . We describe the algorithm in the simpler setting where Alice holds only negative records, Bob holds only positive records, and their feature supports are disjoint ( Lemma 3.5 handles overlapping supports, and Corollary 3.13 extends the algorithm to mixed labels.) Also, recall that thresholds label points below their respective cutoffs as negative and those at or above as positive (see Equation 4 ). For thresholds with | 𝒳 | = m |\mathcal{X}|=m and t ≥ 2 t\geq 2 , we reduce the promise problem to comparing two witness blocks of k = ⌊ t / 2 ⌋ k=\lfloor t/2\rfloor records from the size- n n datasets ( Figure 2 ). We prove a simple structural result that implies that if opt ℋ thr ​ ( S A , S B ) = 0 \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{thr}}}(S_{A},S_{B})=0 , then all of Alice’s points are smaller than all of Bob’s points, and if opt ℋ thr ​ ( S A , S B ) ≥ t \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{thr}}}(S_{A},S_{B})\geq t , then every retained point of Alice exceeds every retained point of Bob. See Figure 2 for intuition. Therefore, k k points are sufficient to distinguish between 𝖬𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁 \mathsf{Match} and 𝖥𝖺𝗋 \mathsf{Far} . Note that if 0 < opt ℋ thr < t 0<\mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{thr}}}<t , both answers can happen, as is standard in distribution testing. Given this reduction, a natural idea is for Alice and Bob to compare their blocks using a privately chosen point. Alice applies the exponential mechanism over the full public domain 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , favoring points near her block’s median, and sends her choice to Bob, who privately counts how many of his records fall below it. Selecting among O ⁡ ( m ) O(m) candidates incurs score error O ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( m ) / ε ) O(\log(m)/\varepsilon) . Taking k k large enough to dominate this error and Bob’s counting noise ensures, with constant failure probability, that Alice’s choice lies within her block’s range and Bob’s comparison identifies the correct order. This yields resolution O ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( m ) / ε ) O(\log(m)/\varepsilon) , but leaves a gap with respect to our Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ log ⁡ ( m ) / ε ) \Omega\bigl(\log\log(m)/\varepsilon\bigr) lower bound. To compare the blocks with a better dependence on m m , we build on the standard Greater-Than protocol for comparing two numbers [ RY20 , Chapter 3] . We adapt its search over prefix lengths to handle blocks of records while preserving privacy. Specifically, we encode each point’s rank in the public domain as a binary string of length b = O ⁡ ( log ⁡ m ) b=O(\log m) and organize these strings into a binary trie; see Figure 3 . Each node at depth ℓ \ell contains the strings sharing a particular prefix of length ℓ \ell . When each party holds a single distinct string, their first differing bit determines their order. Their prefixes agree before that bit and disagree from that bit onward, so binary search locates it using O ⁡ ( log ⁡ b ) = O ⁡ ( log ⁡ log ⁡ m ) O(\log b)=O(\log\log m) prefix-equality tests. At that position, the string with bit 0 0 precedes the string with bit 1 1 . Figure 3 : A binary trie for the ordered witness blocks. A node p p at depth ℓ \ell represents a prefix; A p ℓ A_{p}^{\ell} and B p ℓ B_{p}^{\ell} contain the records in Alice’s and Bob’s blocks with that prefix. Blue and red shading indicate Alice’s and Bob’s records, respectively, and dashed circles mark the common nodes shared by both. Because the blocks are strictly ordered, at most one node at each depth is common. For blocks of records, however, the first separation may involve too few points to overcome privacy noise. We therefore search for a depth at which sufficiently many records have left the shared prefix. To measure this, let A p ℓ A_{p}^{\ell} and B p ℓ B_{p}^{\ell} contain the records in the respective blocks with prefix p ∈ { 0 , 1 } ℓ p\in\{0,1\}^{\ell} , and define M ( ℓ ) := max p min { | A p ℓ | , | B p ℓ | } M(\ell):=\newmax_{p}\newmin\{|A_{p}^{\ell}|,|B_{p}^{\ell}|\} and F ⁡ ( ℓ ) := k − M ⁡ ( ℓ ) F(\ell):=k-M(\ell) . Since the blocks are strictly ordered, at most one node at each depth contains records from both parties. When this common node exists, F ⁡ ( ℓ ) F(\ell) is the larger of the two counts of records outside it. As each child contains only records from its parent, M ⁡ ( ℓ ) M(\ell) cannot increase with depth; consequently, F ⁡ ( ℓ ) F(\ell) is nondecreasing from F ⁡ ( 0 ) = 0 F(0)=0 to F ⁡ ( b ) = k F(b)=k . We can therefore use noisy binary search to find adjacent depths L , H = L + 1 L,H=L+1 whose values of F F bracket a target level α \alpha up to the estimation error, with α \alpha chosen well above that error. To estimate F ⁡ ( ℓ ) F(\ell) without incurring the unwanted log ⁡ m \log m cost, we estimate M ⁡ ( ℓ ) M(\ell) through a small hashed histogram. A direct noisy histogram over all 2 ℓ 2^{\ell} prefixes would incur an error that grows with ℓ \ell , but at most 2 ​ k 2k prefixes are occupied. The parties therefore use the same public hash into O ⁡ ( k 2 / β 0 ) O(k^{2}/\beta_{0}) buckets, which keeps distinct occupied prefixes in different buckets with probability at least 1 − β 0 / 2 1-\beta_{0}/2 . They then add Laplace noise to their bucket counts and take the maximum over buckets of the smaller noisy count. With privacy budget ε 0 \varepsilon_{0} per party, this estimates M ⁡ ( ℓ ) M(\ell) , and hence F ⁡ ( ℓ ) F(\ell) , to error O ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( k / β 0 ) / ε 0 ) O(\log(k/\beta_{0})/\varepsilon_{0}) with failure probability at most β 0 \beta_{0} . The error thus depends logarithmically on k k and 1 / β 0 1/\beta_{0} , rather than on the full prefix universe. These estimates locate a useful depth, but we must still determine which block comes first. If the estimated increase from F ⁡ ( L ) F(L) to F ⁡ ( H ) F(H) is large, the common node at depth L L splits enough records between its two children to reveal the order. Otherwise, F ⁡ ( H ) F(H) is already of order α \alpha , while the common node at depth H H still contains most of each block. The records accumulated outside this node then reveal the order: in 𝖬𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁 \mathsf{Match} , Alice’s lie to its left and Bob’s to its right, with these directions reversed in 𝖥𝖺𝗋 \mathsf{Far} . In both cases, each party computes a comparison statistic from weighted maxima of counts. These statistics have constant sensitivity even when their maximizing prefixes change, and their difference distinguishes the two orders with a margin of Ω ⁡ ( α ) \Omega(\alpha) . We can therefore add noise without identifying the common prefix itself. The search uses only T = ⌈ log 2 ⁡ b ⌉ = O ⁡ ( log ⁡ log ⁡ m ) T=\lceil\log_{2}b\rceil=O(\log\log m) adaptive queries. We give each query a privacy budget ε 0 = ε / ( 2 ​ T ) \varepsilon_{0}=\varepsilon/(2T) and a failure budget β 0 = β / ( 2 ​ T ) \beta_{0}=\beta/(2T) , leaving half of each party’s privacy budget and half of the total failure budget for the final comparison. With these allocations, a margin α = O ⁡ ( ( T / ε ) ​ log ⁡ ( k ​ T / β ) ) \alpha=O\bigl((T/\varepsilon)\log(kT/\beta)\bigr) suffices to dominate the noise in both stages. Taking k ≥ 4 ​ α k\geq 4\alpha makes the final comparisons reliable; since k = ⌊ t / 2 ⌋ k=\lfloor t/2\rfloor , this condition holds when t t is a sufficiently large constant multiple of ( T / ε ) ​ log ⁡ ( T / ( ε ​ β ) ) (T/\varepsilon)\log(T/(\varepsilon\beta)) . Thus, at constant failure probability, we obtain an ε \varepsilon -private tester with resolution t = O ~ ​ ( log ⁡ log ⁡ ( m ) / ε ) t=\tilde{O}\bigl(\log\log(m)/\varepsilon\bigr) , independent of the original dataset size n n , provided n ≥ t n\geq t .

sections.heading: 1.4.3 Algorithm for Halfspaces: Cutting Plane in the Dual Space
sections.text: Figure 4 : The halfspace promise problem viewed in the dual space. Our algorithm works in the dual space and tests which case holds. For the class of halfspaces in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} with | 𝒳 | = m |\mathcal{X}|=m , our main idea is to move to the dual space, where each classifier h w h_{w} is represented by a point w ∈ ℝ d w\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . Since only the predictions on the public domain matter, the Sauer–Shelah lemma allows us to restrict attention to a finite public set of candidate classifiers 𝒲 disc \mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{disc}} of size at most m d m^{d} . Let G A k G_{A}^{k} and G B k G_{B}^{k} denote the candidates that make at most k = ⌊ ( t − 1 ) / ( 2 ​ ( d + 1 ) ) ⌋ k=\lfloor(t-1)/(2(d+1))\rfloor mistakes on Alice’s and Bob’s data, respectively. Unlike the ordered witness blocks for thresholds, these sets of low-error classifiers can be very unstructured. Our key observation is that their convex hulls distinguish the two cases. In 𝖬𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁 \mathsf{Match} , the sets share a consistent classifier w ⋆ w^{\star} . In 𝖥𝖺𝗋 \mathsf{Far} , even their convex hulls are disjoint: conv ⁡ ( G A k ) ∩ conv ⁡ ( G B k ) = ∅ . \displaystyle\mathrm{conv}(G_{A}^{k})\cap\mathrm{conv}(G_{B}^{k})=\emptyset. To see why, suppose a point belongs to both convex hulls. By Carathéodory’s theorem, it is a convex combination of at most d + 1 d+1 low-error classifiers from each party. A convex combination can misclassify a record only if at least one of its constituent classifiers misclassifies that record. Thus, this point would define a classifier with at most 2 ​ ( d + 1 ) ​ k < t 2(d+1)k<t mistakes on the pooled data, contradicting 𝖥𝖺𝗋 \mathsf{Far} . This geometric separation suggests an iterative elimination algorithm, inspired by [ BKMS19 ] . The parties maintain a public set of active candidates. In 𝖥𝖺𝗋 \mathsf{Far} , a hyperplane separates the convex hulls of their remaining low-error classifiers. At least one side of this hyperplane contains at most half of the active candidates. Thus, at least one party has a halfspace cut that retains all of its low-error classifiers while discarding at least half of the candidates. The next challenge is to choose such a cut privately. Searching directly over all possible halfspace cuts would be costly in terms of privacy. Instead, we use halfspace containers [ BKMS19 , DGM22 ] to obtain a small public menu of 2 O ⁡ ( d ) 2^{O(d)} subsets of the active candidates. Whenever a halfspace contains at most half of the active candidates, one of these containers covers its candidates while containing at most 3 / 4 3/4 of the active set. We can therefore search over this small menu while still eliminating a constant fraction of the candidates. Alice and Bob use the exponential mechanism with a low-sensitivity cost to select a container or abstain. With high probability, at least one party selects a shrinking container in each 𝖥𝖺𝗋 \mathsf{Far} round, while every selected container preserves w ⋆ w^{\star} in 𝖬𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁 \mathsf{Match} . Thus, within O ⁡ ( d ​ log ⁡ m ) O(d\log m) rounds, the active set becomes empty in 𝖥𝖺𝗋 \mathsf{Far} and remains nonempty in 𝖬𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁 \mathsf{Match} . Considering all the factors, we can show this algorithm is an ε \varepsilon -private tester with t = O ~ ​ ( d 3 ​ log ⁡ ( m ) / ε ) t=\tilde{O}\bigl(d^{3}\log(m)/\varepsilon\bigr) . Intuitively, the resolution O ~ ​ ( d 3 ​ log ⁡ ( m ) / ε ) \tilde{O}(d^{3}\log(m)/\varepsilon) factors as d ​ log ⁡ m ε ⋅ d ⋅ d \frac{d\log m}{\varepsilon}\cdot d\cdot d , where d ​ log ⁡ m ε \frac{d\log m}{\varepsilon} arises from splitting the privacy budget across O ⁡ ( d ​ log ⁡ m ) O(d\log m) elimination rounds, the second factor of d d is the entropy of the containers that we need to pay due to exponential mechanism, and the third factor of d d comes from Carathéodory theorem when relating the global mistake gap t t to the local error threshold k = Θ ⁡ ( t / d ) k=\Theta(t/d) .

sections.heading: 1.5 Related Work
sections.text: Our work lies at the intersection of three lines of research: communication-efficient distributed learning, testing whether a good model exists without learning one, and data valuation.

sections.heading: Distributed Communication-Efficient Learning.
sections.text: A line of work studies communication-efficient distributed learning [ BBFM12 , CBC16 , KLMY19 ] . Broadly speaking, in the two-party setting, each agent holds a set of labeled examples, and the players communicate to learn a classifier with small error. In much of this work, the algorithms communicate with each other using samples, and the goal is to minimize the number of samples communicated. However, [ BBFM12 ] also propose and analyze the more general setting in which communication can be arbitrary, and the goal is to minimize the total number of bits communicated, possibly subject to privacy constraints. Our setting can be viewed as a property-testing version of the distributed communication-efficient learning problem. More closely related to our halfspace algorithm is the work of [ BKMS19 ] , who study distributed halfspace learning and convex set disjointness over a known finite domain and measure communication in bits. Their goal is to minimize the number of bits exchanged. Our focus is on the smallest resolution t t for testing whether opt ℋ = 0 \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}=0 or opt ℋ ≥ t \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}\geq t under two-party DP. On the technical side, our halfspace algorithm builds on their container approach, using the improved container bounds of [ DGM22 ] . We apply this approach to sets of low-error classifiers in the dual space and select containers privately to eliminate candidates while preserving a shared, consistent classifier when one exists.

sections.heading: Testing and Estimating Learnability.
sections.text: A related line of work asks whether one can test if the optimal population error using classifiers in a hypothesis class is small or large without learning a classifier [ BBBY12 , KNOW14 , BH18 , KV18 ] . In the active testing setting, the learner has access to a large pool of unlabeled samples and chooses which points to label. The goal is to answer this question using as few label queries as possible. A related question with access to i.i.d. labeled samples is studied in [ KV18 ] . Under distributional assumptions, they show that the optimal population loss can be estimated using fewer samples than are needed to learn an accurate predictor. For example, in isotropic regression with suitable moment bounds, they show a quadratic gap in the dependence on dimension: O ⁡ ( d ) O(\sqrt{d}) samples suffice to estimate the optimal squared loss to constant accuracy, whereas learning can require Ω ⁡ ( d ) \Omega(d) samples. They also discuss using such estimates for data valuation and comparing separate and pooled datasets to assess whether joint training is promising. These works share our goal of assessing prediction error without learning a classifier. They focus on using as few labels or samples as possible to assess population error. Our main constraint is privacy: two agents hold labeled datasets and want to determine whether a single classifier in their hypothesis class fits all the pooled records, or whether every classifier makes at least t t mistakes. The challenge is to achieve a small resolution t t while protecting individual records throughout the agents’ interaction. We provide upper and lower bounds on t t that quantify the cost of two-party DP. Similar to this line of work, our threshold result also distinguishes between private testing and private learning. For fixed fractional empirical testing gap, learning accuracy, and confidence, our tester needs only O ~ ​ ( log ⁡ log ⁡ m / ε ) \widetilde{O}(\log\log m/\varepsilon) samples per party, whereas distribution-free pure-private threshold learning requires Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ m / ε ) \Omega(\log m/\varepsilon) samples even with a trusted curator.

sections.heading: Data Valuation and Selection.
sections.text: Data valuation supports decisions throughout the machine learning pipeline, from selecting and pricing training data to debugging trained models [ WYZKJ24 , TLLCJKLR22 , KL17 ] . Popular approaches guide these decisions by assigning scores to individual records or entire datasets using Shapley values or leave-one-out contributions [ GZ19 , JDWHHGLZSS19 , GHVLP24 ] . These methods must, however, account for non-monotonicity, since adding training data can worsen downstream test performance, including when pooling data from heterogeneous sources [ NKBYBS20 , CZPR23 ] . Our opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) > t \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})>t scenario captures a related obstacle when individually realizable datasets admit no shared classifier that fits both perfectly. For data selection, such non-monotonicity can give adaptive methods a strict advantage over fixed score-based methods under equal value-query budgets [ PKFZ26 ] , paralleling the benefit of interaction between agents in private threshold testing noted in Remark 3.4 .

sections.heading: Private Data Appraisal and Valuation.
sections.text: Existing private appraisal methods differ in both what they protect and what their assessments establish. Secure-computation methods, for example, estimate learning gains or Shapley values while permitting leakage through the released appraisal [ XHV22 , TLLCJKLR22 ] . Differential privacy can address such leakage, but its scope varies across methods. Protocols combining homomorphic encryption with label differential privacy leave features public [ ALZK23 ] , while private KNN-based valuation assumes a trusted server and excludes validation-data privacy [ WZWJM23 ] . Similar asymmetries arise in dataset valuation that protects sellers without providing corresponding guarantees for the buyer [ JMMC24 ] . Protecting both sides therefore remains a challenge, as broader analyses of private valuation also emphasize [ FWC26 ] . Beyond these privacy constraints, the assessment itself may not certify compatibility. Similarity-based methods estimate dataset divergence or correlation without establishing whether a shared classifier fits the combined data [ FXC25 , CPP23 , JMMC24 ] . Likewise, protecting fixed valuation scores does not itself ensure that they identify useful data combinations [ PKFZ26 ] . These limitations leave unresolved the worst-case accuracy limits of compatibility testing under two-party record-level differential privacy without a trusted curator or computational assumptions.

sections.heading: 2.2 Two-Party DP and Connection to Information Complexity
sections.text: In an interactive protocol, privacy must hold not only for the final 𝖬𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁 \mathsf{Match} or 𝖥𝖺𝗋 \mathsf{Far} output, but for the entire interaction transcript observed by each party. For a protocol Π \Pi and inputs ( S A , S B ) (S_{A},S_{B}) , let View A Π ​ ( S A , S B ) \mathrm{View}_{A}^{\Pi}(S_{A},S_{B}) denote Alice’s complete view of the execution, consisting of her input S A S_{A} , her private randomness, the public randomness, all exchanged messages, and the common output; define View B Π ​ ( S A , S B ) \mathrm{View}_{B}^{\Pi}(S_{A},S_{B}) similarly. Definition 2.1 (Differential privacy for two-party protocols [ MMPRTV10 ] ) . A two-party protocol Π \Pi is ε \varepsilon -differentially private if each party’s view is ε \varepsilon -differentially private with respect to the other party’s dataset. More precisely, for every fixed S A S_{A} , every pair of neighboring datasets S B , S B ′ S_{B},S_{B}^{\prime} , and every measurable event E E , Pr [ View A Π ( S A , S B ) ∈ E ] ≤ e ε Pr [ View A Π ( S A , S B ′ ) ∈ E ] , \displaystyle\Pr\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathrm{View}_{A}^{\Pi}(S_{A},S_{B})\in E}}\right]\leq e^{\varepsilon}\Pr\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathrm{View}_{A}^{\Pi}(S_{A},S_{B}^{\prime})\in E}}\right], and, symmetrically, for every fixed S B S_{B} , every pair of neighboring datasets S A , S A ′ S_{A},S_{A}^{\prime} , and every measurable event E E , Pr [ View B Π ( S A , S B ) ∈ E ] ≤ e ε Pr [ View B Π ( S A ′ , S B ) ∈ E ] . \displaystyle\Pr\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathrm{View}_{B}^{\Pi}(S_{A},S_{B})\in E}}\right]\leq e^{\varepsilon}\Pr\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathrm{View}_{B}^{\Pi}(S_{A}^{\prime},S_{B})\in E}}\right]. We require differential privacy on the full input domain, including inputs that do not satisfy the promise of the testing problem. We also make a repeated use of this lemma which is a simple modification of the connection between DP and internal information complexity from [ MMPRTV10 ] . Lemma 2.2 . Let 𝒜 \mathcal{A} and ℬ \mathcal{B} be finite sets, and let E A : 𝒜 → 𝒳 n E_{A}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{X}^{n} and E B : ℬ → 𝒳 n E_{B}:\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{X}^{n} be deterministic maps that encode inputs in 𝒜 \mathcal{A} and ℬ \mathcal{B} as size- n n datasets over 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . Define the encoding diameter of E A E_{A} and E B E_{B} as follows: Δ A := max a , a ′ ∈ 𝒜 d ham ( E A ( a ) , E A ( a ′ ) ) , Δ B := max b , b ′ ∈ ℬ d ham ( E B ( b ) , E B ( b ′ ) ) . \displaystyle\Delta_{A}:=\newmax_{a,a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\mathrm{d}_{\text{ham}}\bigl(E_{A}(a),E_{A}(a^{\prime})\bigr),\qquad\Delta_{B}:=\newmax_{b,b^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}}\mathrm{d}_{\text{ham}}\bigl(E_{B}(b),E_{B}(b^{\prime})\bigr). Suppose ( A , B ) ∼ μ (A,B)\sim\mu for a distribution μ \mu over 𝒜 × ℬ \mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{B} , and Alice and Bob execute an ε \varepsilon -differentially private protocol Π \Pi on the encoded datasets ( E A ​ ( A ) , E B ​ ( B ) ) \bigl(E_{A}(A),E_{B}(B)\bigr) . Let T T denote the resulting public transcript (consisting of the public randomness, all exchanged messages, and the final output). Then the internal information cost of T T (in bits) satisfies I ⁡ ( A ; T ∣ B ) + I ⁡ ( B ; T ∣ A ) ≤ ε ⁡ ( Δ A + Δ B ) ln ⁡ 2 . \displaystyle I(A;T\mid B)+I(B;T\mid A)\leq\frac{\varepsilon(\Delta_{A}+\Delta_{B})}{\ln 2}.

sections.heading: 3.1 Lower bound for thresholds
sections.text: The next result presents a fundamental lower bound on t t for the class of thresholds. The main idea is to embed a binary function with a high information complexity and then use the connection between information complexity and two-view DP from [ MMPRTV10 ] to provide a lower bound. Theorem 3.1 (Lower bound for thresholds) . There exist universal constants c > 0 c>0 and m 0 ∈ ℕ m_{0}\in\mathbb{N} such that the following holds. For every m ≥ m 0 m\geq m_{0} , every 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ \mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R} with | 𝒳 | = m |\mathcal{X}|=m , every ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 , and every n , t ∈ ℕ n,t\in\mathbb{N} such that t ≤ n t\leq n , we have that every ε \varepsilon -private tester for ℋ thr \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{thr}} with resolution t t for dataset of size n n (from Definition 1.2 ) requires t ≥ c ​ log ⁡ log ⁡ m ε . \displaystyle t\geq c\frac{\log\log m}{\varepsilon}. Remark 3.2 . Fix ε ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \varepsilon\in(0,1] and n ∈ ℕ n\in\mathbb{N} . Theorem 3.1 implies that no ε \varepsilon -private tester for thresholds over ℝ \mathbb{R} at dataset size n n can achieve a resolution 1 ≤ t ≤ n 1\leq t\leq n . Indeed, restricting such a tester to a finite domain of size m m would give t ≥ c ​ log ⁡ log ⁡ ( m ) / ε t\geq c\log\log(m)/\varepsilon for arbitrarily large m m , contradicting the fact that t t is fixed. A trusted curator can achieve resolution t = O ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) t=O(1/\varepsilon) , independently of the domain size, by adding Laplace noise to the sensitivity-one quantity opt \mathrm{opt} . This resolution is nontrivial provided n ≥ C / ε n\geq C/\varepsilon for a sufficiently large universal constant C C . Thus, on finite domains of size m m , the two-party setting incurs an unavoidable multiplicative Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ log ⁡ m ) \Omega(\log\log m) overhead relative to the centralized resolution. Remark 3.3 . Under cryptographic assumptions, secure function evaluation can emulate the trusted curator and achieve t = O ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) t=O(1/\varepsilon) with computational differential privacy [ MMPRTV10 ] . However, Theorem 3.1 shows that information-theoretic view-based privacy requires OPEN t = Ω ​ ( log ⁡ log ⁡ ( m ) / ε CLOSE ) t=\Omega\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\log\log(m)/{\varepsilon}}}\right) . Thus, the two models exhibit a separation in the achievable promise gap. Remark 3.4 . The lower bound in Theorem 3.1 allows arbitrary interaction between Alice and Bob. For one-way protocols with bounded worst-case error, however, the standard information-theoretic argument underlying the Greater-Than lower bound [ RY20 , Chapter 6] shows that Alice’s message must reveal Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ m ) \Omega(\log m) bits about her input when it is uniformly random. Indeed, given any prefix of Alice’s input, Bob can choose a comparison that predicts her next bit with constant error; Fano’s inequality and the chain rule then give the information lower bound. Applying this argument to the encoding in Theorem 3.1 , group privacy bounds the information revealed by Alice’s message by O ⁡ ( ε ​ t ) O(\varepsilon t) , yielding t = Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( m ) / ε ) t=\Omega(\log(m)/\varepsilon) . The private-interior-point baseline in Section 3.2.3 achieves the matching O ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( m ) / ε ) O(\log(m)/\varepsilon) resolution. Thus, interaction is necessary to achieve our improved resolution of O ~ ​ ( log ⁡ log ​ ( m ) / ε ) \widetilde{O}(\log\log(m)/\varepsilon) . Proof of Theorem 3.1 . sections.heading: 4.1 Lower bound for half spaces
sections.text: In this section, we prove an information-theoretic lower bound for ℋ hs \mathcal{H}_{\text{hs}} . The argument for the lower bound is rather technical and it involves many steps. We first provide an overview of the proof and defer the formal proof to Appendix in Appendix D . In this informal overview, we only focus on the case of large n n , i.e., n ≥ C ​ m ​ d ​ log ⁡ ( m / d ) ε n\geq C\frac{md\log(m/d)}{\varepsilon} to highlight main ideas. With slight modifications, we can extend the lower bound to all values of n n as shown in Appendix E and Theorem E.4 .

sections.heading: 4.1.1 Overview of the lower bound proof.
sections.text: The proof follows the same template as that of Theorem 3.1 . We take a binary predicate with high information complexity and embed it into the promise problem, so that the verdict of the promise problem determines the value of the predicate, and then derive the lower bound from the connection between DP and information complexity from [ MMPRTV10 ] . For half spaces, however, constructing an embedding with a sufficiently large gap is substantially more delicate. Our starting viewpoint is that each of Alice’s and Bob’s data points may be read as a linear constraint on w ∈ ℝ d w\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , namely ⟨ w , x ⟩ ≥ 0 \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left<{{{{{w},{x}}}}}}}\right>\geq 0 or ⟨ w , x ⟩ < 0 \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left<{{{{{w},{x}}}}}}}\right><0 . Viewed in the dual space, the problem therefore becomes a linear program with finitely many constraints: in the Match case the system is feasible, whereas in the Far case it remains infeasible even after removing any t − 1 t-1 of the constraints. Achieving this robustness in the Far case is the main technical difficulty of the proof, and it is what leads us to use error-correcting codes.

sections.heading: Step 1: from inner product in a finite field to LP constraints.
sections.text: Let s s be an integer determined later and q = 2 s q=2^{s} . Alice holds a secret u ∈ 𝔽 q k u\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k} and Bob holds a secret v ∈ 𝔽 q k v\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k} , and they wish to compute F ⁡ ( u , v ) = ⨁ i = 1 k Tr 𝔽 q / 𝔽 2 ⁡ ( u i ​ v i ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } . F(u,v)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{k}\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}/\mathbb{F}_{2}}(u_{i}v_{i})\in\{0,1\}. (11) F F can be thought of as the trace of an inner product over 𝔽 q \mathbb{F}_{q} . The internal information complexity of computing F F is Θ ⁡ ( k ​ log ⁡ q ) \Theta(k\log q) ; for completeness we provide a proof in Lemma B.6 . We now build a linear program whose feasibility decides Equation 11 . The main challenge here is that the computation in Equation 11 consists of non-linear components over 𝔽 q \mathbb{F}_{q} while we want to convert it to a feasibility problem in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} . To do so, we embed the q q elements of 𝔽 q \mathbb{F}_{q} as the vertices of a convex polygon P q ⊂ ℝ 2 P_{q}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} lying on a parabola (so each symbol uses two real coordinates) and represent each finite-field relation by the convex hull of its satisfying assignments (for details see Figure 6 ). The resulting LP constraints come in two kinds: A public family , known to both parties and independent of u u and v v , performs the computation itself: it holds the variables in the right ranges, forms the k k trace products, and accumulates their parity, with one last row requiring the parity to be zero. A private family encodes Alice’s and Bob’s secrets: each coordinate of u u and v v contributes exactly one constraint, which we call a pin (the naming is inspired by our way of converting elements of 𝔽 q \mathbb{F}_{q} into a linear program in Figure 6 ). Once all 2 ​ k 2k of these are present, the fixed rows propagate the computation and the program is feasible if and only if F ⁡ ( u , v ) = 0 F(u,v)=0 . We give the details of constructing such a program in Appendix D . Reading this back through Definition 1.2 , we obtain a Match instance whenever F ⁡ ( u , v ) = 0 F(u,v)=0 and a Far instance whenever F ⁡ ( u , v ) = 1 F(u,v)=1 . This feasibility equivalence alone certifies only a Far gap of one. Repeating each linear constraint L L times guarantees opt ℋ hs ≥ L \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{hs}}}\geq L , but the encoding diameter of Lemma 2.2 rises to 2 ​ k ​ L 2kL . Then, by the connection of the IC and encoding diameter from Lemma 2.2 , we obtain only t = Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ q / ε ) t=\Omega(\log q/\varepsilon) . The shortcoming of the simple repetition is that the Far gap grows only with the replication L L , while the diameter grows with k ​ L kL . Can we instead design a program that is already robust to deleting D ≥ 1 D\geq 1 of its private pins (i.e., erasing D D symbols) before any replication?

sections.heading: Step 2: turning code robustness into LP rigidity.
sections.text: What we need is that, as long as the public constraints remain enforced, removing fewer than D D pins still leaves the final answer intact. We therefore encode u u and v v using a public systematic linear code with generator G = [ 𝕀 k ∣ A ] ∈ 𝔽 q k × K G=[\mathbb{I}_{k}\mid A]\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k\times K} where K > k K>k . Let c = u ​ G c=uG and c ′ = v ​ G c^{\prime}=vG ; since the code is systematic, the first k k coordinates of c c and c ′ c^{\prime} are u u and v v themselves, so the trace products of Equation 11 are still formed from these coordinates alone. Three properties are needed from the code and its parity-check representation: constant rate, so that k = Θ ⁡ ( K ) k=\Theta(K) ; linear LP-erasure rigidity , meaning the LP tolerates up to D = Θ ⁡ ( K ) D=\Theta(K) removed pins; and constant check degree, for a reason that will become clear below. The key subtlety is that local parity-check constraints only enforce a convex relaxation of the code, which can admit fractional solutions even when the code has large minimum distance. We therefore use a code whose parity-check graph is a constant-degree unique-neighbor expander [ FWK05 ] : whenever fewer than D = Θ ⁡ ( K ) D=\Theta(K) pins are removed, any nonempty set of unpinned coordinates has an adjacent check touching it in a single coordinate, whose remaining pinned coordinates force that variable back to its true symbol ( Lemma C.2 ). Thus the public constraints still uniquely force c c and c ′ c^{\prime} . Two counts govern the size of the construction, and separating them is what makes a large alphabet affordable. First, since each 𝔽 q \mathbb{F}_{q} symbol is embedded in ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} , the program uses d LP := 4 ​ K + 2 ​ k + 1 = Θ ⁡ ( K ) d_{\mathrm{LP}}:=4K+2k+1=\Theta(K) variables ( 2 ​ K 2K per codeword, k k trace, and k + 1 k+1 parity variables), independent of q q , allowing us to choose K = Θ ⁡ ( d ) K=\Theta(d) . Second, each distinct LP inequality corresponds to a point in the public data space 𝒳 \mathcal{X} of size m m . Because each check involves only ρ = O ⁡ ( 1 ) \rho=O(1) symbols, its convex hull in ℝ 2 ​ ρ \mathbb{R}^{2\rho} is described by q O ⁡ ( ρ 2 ) = q O ⁡ ( 1 ) q^{O(\rho^{2})}=q^{O(1)} inequalities; across all O ⁡ ( K ) O(K) checks and computation gates, this yields at most C ​ K ​ q a CKq^{a} distinct records for universal constants C , a C,a (replication increases multiplicities, not distinct records). The alphabet therefore costs records but never dimensions, which is what will let us take q q large.

sections.heading: 4.2.2 Main Algorithm
sections.text: In this section, we present the algorithm for half spaces. We begin with providing an overview of the technical ideas.

sections.heading: Overview of the algorithm.
sections.text: Our algorithm is a private elimination procedure over the finite dual space 𝒲 disc \mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{disc}} . At round r r , the parties maintain a public set 𝒲 r \mathcal{W}_{r} of candidate halfspaces and attempt to replace it by a substantially smaller set. Ideally, a party would find a halfspace in the dual space that contains all of its low-error candidates but at most half of 𝒲 r \mathcal{W}_{r} . Such a halfspace defines a safe cut, but the family of possible halfspaces is too large to search privately. The container lemma in Lemma 4.5 replaces these halfspace cuts by a small public family: whenever such a halfspace exists, the family contains a set covering it and containing at most 3 ​ | 𝒲 r | / 4 3|\mathcal{W}_{r}|/4 candidates. For P ∈ { A , B } P\in\{A,B\} , let G P k ​ ( 𝒲 r ) G_{P}^{k}(\mathcal{W}_{r}) denote the candidates in 𝒲 r \mathcal{W}_{r} with local error at most k k . We assign each container a low-sensitivity cost measuring the quality of the best halfspace candidate it excludes; its cost is zero exactly when it contains all of G P k ​ ( 𝒲 r ) G_{P}^{k}(\mathcal{W}_{r}) . Alice and Bob can therefore use the exponential mechanism to privately search the public container family for a safe shrinking cut. The high level goal is as follows: The two promise cases interact with this mechanism in opposite ways, and the stopping rule reads off which occurred: a Match instance keeps 𝒲 r \mathcal{W}_{r} nonempty forever, while a Far instance is driven to 𝒲 r = ∅ \mathcal{W}_{r}=\emptyset within OPEN log ⁡ ( | 𝒲 disc | CLOSE ) \log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(|\mathcal{W}_{\text{disc}}|}}\right) rounds, thanks to Lemma 4.3 that shows | 𝒲 disc | |\mathcal{W}_{\text{disc}}| is finite.

sections.heading: Far case.

sections.heading: 4.2.3 Complementary bounds for small data regime
sections.text: An interesting aspect of the guarantee in Theorem 4.7 is that t t does not depend on the dataset size n n . However, the cost of such a result is that we need OPEN n ≥ O ~ ​ ( d 3 ​ log ⁡ ( m ) ε CLOSE ) n\geq\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d^{3}\log(m)}{\varepsilon}}}\right) . In this section, we show that when n n is small, there are simple algorithms that extend the private tester to almost all non-trivial dataset sizes.

sections.heading: A tester with t = n t=n .
sections.text: In this section, we give a simple algorithm to show that, as long as n ≳ 1 / ε 2 n\gtrsim 1/\varepsilon^{2} , we can design a tester that achieves t = n t=n . Note that this is the largest resolution one can ask for: classifier w = 0 w=0 labels every point as positive and makes exactly n n mistakes, and therefore opt ℋ hs ​ ( S A , S B ) ≤ n \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{hs}}}(S_{A},S_{B})\leq n for all datasets. The starting point is a simple characterization of when opt ℋ hs ​ ( S A , S B ) = n \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{hs}}}(S_{A},S_{B})=n . Note that we assume the homogeneous halfspaces in Equation 10 without a bias term. For x ≠ 0 x\neq 0 , let R ⁡ ( x ) = { λ ​ x : λ > 0 } R(x)=\{\lambda x:\lambda>0\} denote the ray through x x , and let ℛ = { R ⁡ ( x ) : x ∈ 𝒳 } \mathcal{R}=\{R(x):x\in\mathcal{X}\} be the set of rays that contain at least one point of the domain. Since the domain is finite, this set is well-defined. Notice that ℛ \mathcal{R} is public. For every R ∈ ℛ R\in\mathcal{R} , let a R a_{R} and b R b_{R} denote the number of Alice’s and Bob’s records that lie on R R , respectively. The main observation is that a homogeneous halfspace assigns the same label to all the points on a ray. Using this observation, it is straightforward to see that opt ℋ hs ​ ( S A , S B ) = n \displaystyle\mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{hs}}}(S_{A},S_{B})=n ⇔ a R = b R ​ for all ​ R ∈ ℛ , \displaystyle\iff a_{R}=b_{R}~\text{for all}~R\in\mathcal{R}, (14) opt ℋ hs ​ ( S A , S B ) = 0 \displaystyle\mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{hs}}}(S_{A},S_{B})=0 ⟹ a R ​ b R = 0 ​ for all ​ R ∈ ℛ . \displaystyle\implies a_{R}b_{R}=0~\text{for all}~R\in\mathcal{R}. In other words, in the Far case Alice and Bob have exactly the same histogram over the rays, while in the Match case their histograms have disjoint supports. Therefore, at t = n t=n the testing problem reduces to checking whether two histograms over ℛ \mathcal{R} are identical, and this can be done using shared randomness as we show in Algorithm 4 . The next theorem summarize the privacy and utility guarantee of this tester. There exists a universal constant C > 0 C>0 such that the following holds. Fix a finite data space 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ d ∖ { 0 } \mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\} and ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 , and let n ≥ C / ε 2 n\geq C/\varepsilon^{2} . Then there exists a non-interactive algorithm (presented in Algorithm 4 ) that is ε \varepsilon -private tester with resolution t = n t=n for ℋ hs \mathcal{H}_{\text{hs}} . Remark 4.10 (Mixed labels) . Our tester at resolution t = n t=n also applies when each agent holds both positive and negative examples. We retain the assumption that 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ d ∖ { 0 } \mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\} , and write N − N_{-} for the total number of negatively labeled records across the two datasets. Unlike the disjoint-label setting, this number need not equal n n . We first observe that the all-positive classifier makes exactly N − N_{-} mistakes. Thus, in the Far case, we must have N − ≥ n N_{-}\geq n . This suggests a simple first step: each agent releases a noisy count of its negative records, and the agents add these counts. If N − < n / 2 N_{-}<n/2 , this already distinguishes the input from Far, using the threshold 3 ​ n / 4 3n/4 . It remains to handle the case in which there are at least n / 2 n/2 negative records. For this case, we modify the random signs used by the tester. Independently for each line through the origin meeting 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , we assign a random sign to one ray and the opposite sign to the other. Let σ R \sigma_{R} denote the sign assigned to ray R R . Each agent P P releases a noisy version of Z P = ∑ ( x , y ) ∈ S P y ​ σ R ⁡ ( x ) , \displaystyle Z_{P}=\sum_{(x,y)\in S_{P}}y\,\sigma_{R(x)}, and the agents add their releases. Thus, the contribution of a record depends on both its ray and its label. The main observation is that these contributions cancel in the Far case. Indeed, when opt = n \mathrm{opt}=n , every normal orthogonal to no domain point gives exactly n n errors. Moving the normal across the hyperplane perpendicular to one line shows that the positive-label count minus the negative-label count must agree on its two rays. Since these rays receive opposite signs, their contributions sum to zero. In the Match case, consider a line containing a negative record. A classifier realizing the pooled data must place all negative records on this line on one ray and all positive records on the opposite ray. Consequently, multiplying by the labels makes all contributions from this line have the same sign. Since the signs on different lines are independent, the pooled sketch has variance at least N − ≥ n / 2 N_{-}\geq n/2 . The same moment argument as before therefore gives a sketch of magnitude at least n / 2 \sqrt{n}/2 with constant probability. We repeat the sketch a constant number of times. Replacing one labeled record changes each sketch by at most two and the negative-label count by at most one, so Laplace noise of scale O ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) O(1/\varepsilon) suffices for privacy. Combining the count test with the sketches gives an ε \varepsilon -private tester whenever n ≥ C / ε 2 n\geq C/\varepsilon^{2} , for 0 < ε ≤ 1 0<\varepsilon\leq 1 and a universal constant C C , independently of d d and m m .

sections.heading: A tester using private synthetic data generation.
sections.text: A simple application of the mechanism in [ BLR13 ] gives a complementary bound with a better dependence on the dimension. The idea is to have each party privately release a small synthetic dataset that approximates its empirical error for every halfspace. Then, using it, we can approximate opt \mathrm{opt} . Theorem 4.11 (Halfspace testing via the BLR net mechanism) . There exists a universal constant C > 0 C>0 such that the following holds. Fix d ≥ 1 d\geq 1 , m , n ∈ ℕ m,n\in\mathbb{N} , and ε ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \varepsilon\in(0,1] . For every public data space 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ d \mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} with | 𝒳 | = m |\mathcal{X}|=m and every t ∈ [ n ] t\in[n] satisfying OPEN t ≥ C ⁡ ( n 2 ​ d ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ m ) ε CLOSE ) 1 / 3 , t\geq C\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{n^{2}d\log(2m)}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{1/3}, (15) there exists a non-interactive, randomized, ε \varepsilon -two-party DP tester for ℋ hs \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{hs}} with resolution t t . Remark 4.12 . At first glance, the dependence on d d , log ⁡ m \log m , and 1 / ε 1/\varepsilon in Theorem 4.11 scales as ( d ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ m ) ε ) 1 / 3 \bigl(\frac{d\log(2m)}{\varepsilon}\bigr)^{1/3} , which might appear to contradict our lower bound of t = Ω ⁡ ( d ​ log ⁡ ( m / d ) ε ) t=\Omega\bigl(\frac{d\log(m/d)}{\varepsilon}\bigr) from Theorem 4.1 . However, there is no contradiction because the bound in Equation 15 also depends on n n and can be written as a weighted geometric mean of n n and d ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ m ) ε \frac{d\log(2m)}{\varepsilon} : OPEN OPEN ( n 2 ​ d ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ m ) ε CLOSE ) 1 / 3 = n 2 / 3 ​ ( d ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ m ) ε CLOSE ) 1 / 3 . \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{n^{2}d\log(2m)}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{1/3}=n^{2/3}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{d\log(2m)}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{1/3}. Recall that any non-trivial tester requires t ≤ n t\leq n (since opt ℋ hs ​ ( S A , S B ) ≤ n \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{hs}}}(S_{A},S_{B})\leq n holds trivially for all datasets of size n n ). For the right-hand side of Equation 15 to be at most n n , we must have n ≳ d ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ m ) ε n\gtrsim\frac{d\log(2m)}{\varepsilon} . In this regime, the geometric mean always lies between d ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ m ) ε \frac{d\log(2m)}{\varepsilon} and n n , namely OPEN d ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ m ) ε ≲ ( n 2 ​ d ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ m ) ε CLOSE ) 1 / 3 ≤ n . \displaystyle\frac{d\log(2m)}{\varepsilon}\lesssim\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{n^{2}d\log(2m)}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{1/3}\leq n. Conversely, when n ≪ d ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ m ) ε n\ll\frac{d\log(2m)}{\varepsilon} , the right-hand side of Equation 15 exceeds n n , so the range of admissible t ∈ [ n ] t\in[n] in Theorem 4.11 is empty. Thus, whenever Theorem 4.11 is non-vacuous, its resolution t t is always consistent with Theorem 4.1 .

sections.heading: C Embedding a codeword into an LP
sections.text: In this section, we develop the machinery that turns a pair of codewords into an instance of the promise problem. Recall from Section 4.1.1 that each data point imposes one linear constraint on w w , so that opt ℋ hs = 0 \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{hs}}}=0 means the resulting system is feasible, while opt ℋ hs ≥ t \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{hs}}}\geq t means it remains infeasible even after removing any t − 1 t-1 constraints. Our goal is therefore a linear program whose feasibility encodes the value of a hard function, and in which each private symbol contributes exactly one inequality. Our representation is based on the fundamental-polytope approach from the literature on LP decoding of linear codes [ FWK05 , FSBG09 ] . In that approach, each row of a parity-check matrix is represented by the convex hull of its satisfying local assignments, and the resulting local polytopes are intersected to obtain an LP relaxation of the code. We adapt this machinery in two ways. First, we represent every symbol of 𝔽 q \mathbb{F}_{q} as an exposed vertex of a two-dimensional polygon, rather than using the standard indicator representation. Second, we interpret the symbol-selecting inequalities as private data records and the parity-check inequalities as public records.

sections.heading: The function we want to compute.
sections.text: Fix the public parity-check matrix H ∈ 𝔽 q M × K H\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{M\times K} with M = K / 2 M=K/2 , retaining all its rows, and let 𝒞 H = { c ∈ 𝔽 q K : H ​ c ⊤ = 0 } \mathcal{C}_{H}=\{c\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{K}:Hc^{\top}=0\} have dimension k k . We assume that the code is systematic, i.e., the first k k coordinates carry the message and the remaining K − k K-k are determined by the checks. Alice holds a codeword c ∈ 𝒞 H c\in\mathcal{C}_{H} , Bob holds a codeword c ′ ∈ 𝒞 H c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{H} , and they wish to compute F ⁡ ( c , c ′ ) = ⨁ i ∈ [ k ] Tr ⁡ ( c i ​ c i ′ ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } , \displaystyle F(c,c^{\prime})=\bigoplus_{i\in[k]}\operatorname{Tr}(c_{i}c_{i}^{\prime})\in\{0,1\}, where Tr \operatorname{Tr} denotes the trace from 𝔽 q \mathbb{F}_{q} to 𝔽 2 \mathbb{F}_{2} . The computation has three parts: each party’s input must be a genuine codeword, that is, satisfy every parity check of H H ; for every message coordinate i ∈ [ k ] i\in[k] , the bit Tr ⁡ ( c i ​ c i ′ ) \operatorname{Tr}(c_{i}c_{i}^{\prime}) must be computed from the pair ( c i , c i ′ ) (c_{i},c_{i}^{\prime}) ; and these k k bits must be combined by parity. We then plant a public condition on the output, namely that the resulting parity equals zero. Feasibility of the whole system is then equivalent to F ⁡ ( c , c ′ ) = 0 F(c,c^{\prime})=0 .

sections.text: Fix an enumeration 𝔽 q = { α 0 , … , α q − 1 } \mathbb{F}_{q}=\{\alpha_{0},\ldots,\alpha_{q-1}\} and set e ⁡ ( α j ) := ( j , j 2 ) ∈ ℝ 2 e(\alpha_{j}):=(j,j^{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2} . The displayed identity is immediate. Since z i ∈ P q z_{i}\in P_{q} , we may write z i = ∑ s λ s ​ e ​ ( α s ) z_{i}=\sum_{s}\lambda_{s}e(\alpha_{s}) with λ s ≥ 0 \lambda_{s}\geq 0 and ∑ s λ s = 1 \sum_{s}\lambda_{s}=1 . As ℓ j \ell_{j} is linear, ℓ j ​ ( z i ) = ∑ s λ s ​ ℓ j ​ ( e ⁡ ( α s ) ) = j 2 − ∑ s λ s ​ ( s − j ) 2 . \displaystyle\ell_{j}(z_{i})=\sum_{s}\lambda_{s}\,\ell_{j}\bigl(e(\alpha_{s})\bigr)=j^{2}-\sum_{s}\lambda_{s}(s-j)^{2}. sections.heading: Imposing a public relation.
sections.text: The pins determine each symbol individually, but we also need to impose relations among several variables, such as a parity check or the trace of a product. Such relations are not linear, so we cannot write them directly. The following device converts any finite relation into linear inequalities. Let ℛ \mathcal{R} be a public finite set of tuples ( a 1 , … , a r , b 1 , … , b r ′ ) ∈ 𝔽 q r × { 0 , 1 } r ′ (a_{1},\ldots,a_{r},b_{1},\ldots,b_{r^{\prime}})\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{r}\times\{0,1\}^{r^{\prime}} , listing the assignments we wish to allow. Replace each field symbol a i a_{i} by the point e ⁡ ( a i ) e(a_{i}) , we describe the construction above, and leave the bits unchanged. Then, let Q ℛ Q_{\mathcal{R}} be the convex hull of the resulting points in ℝ 2 ​ r + r ′ \mathbb{R}^{2r+r^{\prime}} . These points are rational, so Q ℛ Q_{\mathcal{R}} is a rational polytope and admits a finite description by linear inequalities, which we add to the linear program as public rows. If the polytope is lower-dimensional, this description includes equations for its affine hull, each written as two inequalities. This also covers q = 2 q=2 . In the linear program this reads ( z 1 , … , z r , β 1 , … , β r ′ ) ∈ Q ℛ , \displaystyle(z_{1},\ldots,z_{r},\;\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{r^{\prime}})\in Q_{\mathcal{R}}, where the z i z_{i} are symbol variables and the β j \beta_{j} are real variables playing the role of bits. By itself this constraint is weak, as it says only that the tuple is some mixture of allowed assignments. The point is that pinning some of the variables collapses the mixture. Lemma C.2 (Forced relation) . Fix nonnegative integers r , r ′ r,r^{\prime} with r + r ′ > 0 r+r^{\prime}>0 , and use the convention [ 0 ] = ∅ [0]=\varnothing . Let ℛ ⊆ 𝔽 q r × { 0 , 1 } r ′ \mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{r}\times\{0,1\}^{r^{\prime}} be a finite relation and let Q ℛ Q_{\mathcal{R}} be as above. Fix index sets S ⊆ [ r ] S\subseteq[r] and S ′ ⊆ [ r ′ ] S^{\prime}\subseteq[r^{\prime}] , together with symbols a i ∈ 𝔽 q a_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q} for i ∈ S i\in S and bits b j ∈ { 0 , 1 } b_{j}\in\{0,1\} for j ∈ S ′ j\in S^{\prime} , and suppose that ℛ \mathcal{R} contains exactly one tuple 𝒯 ⋆ \mathcal{T}^{\star} whose i i -th symbol equals a i a_{i} for every i ∈ S i\in S and whose j j th bit equals b j b_{j} for every j ∈ S ′ j\in S^{\prime} . If a point ( z , β ) ∈ Q ℛ (z,\beta)\in Q_{\mathcal{R}} satisfies z i = e ⁡ ( a i ) z_{i}=e(a_{i}) for every i ∈ S i\in S and β j = b j \beta_{j}=b_{j} for every j ∈ S ′ j\in S^{\prime} , then ( z , β ) (z,\beta) equals the point generated by 𝒯 ⋆ \mathcal{T}^{\star} ; in particular every remaining coordinate is forced to the value it takes in 𝒯 ⋆ \mathcal{T}^{\star} . Proof. We want to show that in any convex decomposition of ( z , β ) (z,\beta) over the generating points, all the weight sits on the single generator coming from 𝒯 ⋆ \mathcal{T}^{\star} . Write ( z , β ) = ∑ 𝒯 ∈ ℛ λ 𝒯 ​ v 𝒯 (z,\beta)=\sum_{\mathcal{T}\in\mathcal{R}}\lambda_{\mathcal{T}}\,v_{\mathcal{T}} with λ 𝒯 ≥ 0 \lambda_{\mathcal{T}}\geq 0 and ∑ 𝒯 λ 𝒯 = 1 \sum_{\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{\mathcal{T}}=1 , where v 𝒯 v_{\mathcal{T}} denotes the point generated by the tuple 𝒯 \mathcal{T} . Define L := ∑ i ∈ S ℓ a i + ∑ j ∈ S ′ σ b j , σ 0 ( β ) := − β , σ 1 ( β ) := β , \displaystyle L:=\sum_{i\in S}\ell_{a_{i}}+\sum_{j\in S^{\prime}}\sigma_{b_{j}},\qquad\sigma_{0}(\beta):=-\beta,\quad\sigma_{1}(\beta):=\beta, where ℓ α j \ell_{\alpha_{j}} denotes ℓ j \ell_{j} , ℓ a i \ell_{a_{i}} acts on the i i th symbol block and σ b j \sigma_{b_{j}} on the j j th bit coordinate. By Lemma C.1 , ℓ a i \ell_{a_{i}} is maximized over { e ⁡ ( α ) : α ∈ 𝔽 q } \{e(\alpha):\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\} exactly at e ⁡ ( a i ) e(a_{i}) , and clearly σ b j \sigma_{b_{j}} is maximized over { 0 , 1 } \{0,1\} exactly at b j b_{j} . Writing M M for the resulting maximum, we therefore have L ⁡ ( v 𝒯 ) ≤ M L(v_{\mathcal{T}})\leq M for every 𝒯 ∈ ℛ \mathcal{T}\in\mathcal{R} , with equality if and only if 𝒯 \mathcal{T} agrees with the fixed assignment on S ∪ S ′ S\cup S^{\prime} . On the other hand L ⁡ ( z , β ) = M L(z,\beta)=M by hypothesis, so linearity gives ∑ 𝒯 λ 𝒯 ​ ( M − L ⁡ ( v 𝒯 ) ) = 0 . \displaystyle\sum_{\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl(M-L(v_{\mathcal{T}})\bigr)=0.
