sections.heading: The four families of constraints.
sections.text: We can now assemble the linear program. Every part of the computation becomes an instance of the device above, and the private inputs enter through the pins alone. Symbols. For every i ∈ [ K ] i\in[K] we introduce z i ∈ ℝ 2 z_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} with z i ∈ P q z_{i}\in P_{q} , and Alice’s private input contributes the pin forcing z i = e ⁡ ( c i ) z_{i}=e(c_{i}) . Bob contributes an identical family for a second collection z 1 ′ , … , z K ′ z_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,z_{K}^{\prime} . Parity checks. For every row a a of H H , we take ℛ \mathcal{R} to be the set of assignments to the coordinates in the support of a a that satisfy the check, and impose membership in the corresponding polytope. Applying this to both collections guarantees that pinned inputs are codewords. Trace products. For every i ∈ [ k ] i\in[k] we introduce a real variable r i r_{i} and take ℛ = { ( a , b , Tr ( a b ) ) : a , b ∈ 𝔽 q } \mathcal{R}=\{(a,b,\operatorname{Tr}(ab)):a,b\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\} . Once z i z_{i} and z i ′ z_{i}^{\prime} are pinned, Lemma C.2 forces r i = Tr ⁡ ( c i ​ c i ′ ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } r_{i}=\operatorname{Tr}(c_{i}c_{i}^{\prime})\in\{0,1\} . Parity of the bits. We introduce p 0 , … , p k p_{0},\ldots,p_{k} , impose the public row p 0 = 0 p_{0}=0 , and for every j ∈ [ k ] j\in[k] take ℛ \mathcal{R} to be the four even-parity binary triples, so that the constraint reads ( p j − 1 , r j , p j ) ∈ Q ⊕ (p_{j-1},r_{j},p_{j})\in Q_{\oplus} . Once p j − 1 p_{j-1} and r j r_{j} are bits, Lemma C.2 forces p j = p j − 1 ⊕ r j p_{j}=p_{j-1}\oplus r_{j} . Finally we plant the public row p k = 0 p_{k}=0 . Notice that these families are not independent: the pins force the symbols, the symbols force the trace bits, and the trace bits together with the running parities force the next parity. Each gadget produces integral values only because the previous one already has, so the constraints must be read as a chain rather than as a set.

sections.heading: Size of the embedding.
sections.text: Lemma C.3 (Dimension and number of rows) . The linear program above uses 4 ​ K + 2 ​ k + 1 4K+2k+1 real variables. If H H has M M rows of maximum support size ρ \rho , the public rows together with all candidate private pins admit a rational description using at most O ⁡ ( K ​ q ) + M ​ q O ⁡ ( ρ 2 ) + O ⁡ ( k ​ q 4 + k ) \displaystyle O(Kq)+Mq^{O(\rho^{2})}+O(kq^{4}+k) inequalities. For the chosen ( 4 , 8 ) (4,8) -biregular graph, M = K / 2 M=K/2 and ρ = 8 \rho=8 , so both the public-row count and the full catalogue size are at most B ​ K ​ q a BKq^{a} for universal B , a B,a . Proof. The symbol blocks contribute 4 ​ K 4K variables, the trace bits contribute k k , and the running parities contribute k + 1 k+1 . For the rows, use a rational facet description in each polytope’s affine hull, together with equations defining that affine hull. The Upper Bound Theorem [ McM70 ] bounds the number of facets of a polytope with N N vertices and intrinsic dimension h ≥ 1 h\geq 1 by O h ​ ( N ⌊ h / 2 ⌋ ) O_{h}(N^{\lfloor h/2\rfloor}) . In ambient dimension D D , at most D D affine-hull equations add at most 2 ​ D 2D inequalities; a zero-dimensional polytope needs only these equations. All local ambient dimensions here are bounded by max { 2 ​ ρ , 5 } \newmax\{2\rho,5\} . Symbol constraints and pins. Each of the 2 ​ K 2K symbol blocks uses O ⁡ ( q ) O(q) public inequalities for P q P_{q} , including the affine-hull equation when q = 2 q=2 . Each block has q q possible pins, although only one pin per block is selected for a dataset. Thus the public symbol rows and all 2 ​ K ​ q 2Kq candidate pins use O ⁡ ( K ​ q ) O(Kq) catalogue rows. Parity checks. Fix a check with r a r_{a} nonzero entries. Its valid local assignments are the solutions of one linear equation in r a r_{a} unknowns over 𝔽 q \mathbb{F}_{q} : any r a − 1 r_{a}-1 of the symbols may be chosen freely, and the remaining one is then determined, since its coefficient is nonzero. There are therefore q r a − 1 q^{r_{a}-1} valid assignments, so the associated polytope has at most q r a − 1 q^{r_{a}-1} vertices. Each symbol is represented by a point of ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} , so this polytope lies in dimension at most 2 ​ r a 2r_{a} . Applying the Upper Bound Theorem with N = q r a − 1 N=q^{r_{a}-1} and D = 2 ​ r a D=2r_{a} bounds the facet count by OPEN O ​ ( q r a ​ ( r a − 1 ) CLOSE ) O\!\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(q^{r_{a}(r_{a}-1)}}}\right) ; at most 4 ​ r a 4r_{a} inequalities describe the affine hull. Sum over all M M checks for both words, including redundant checks, to obtain M ​ q O ⁡ ( ρ 2 ) Mq^{O(\rho^{2})} rows. Trace products. The trace polytope is the convex hull of the q 2 q^{2} points ( e ⁡ ( a ) , e ⁡ ( b ) , Tr ⁡ ( a ​ b ) ) \bigl(e(a),e(b),\operatorname{Tr}(ab)\bigr) for a , b ∈ 𝔽 q a,b\in\mathbb{F}_{q} , which lie in ℝ 5 \mathbb{R}^{5} . The Upper Bound Theorem with N = q 2 N=q^{2} and D = 5 D=5 gives O ⁡ ( q 4 ) = q O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(q^{4})=q^{O(1)} facets, and there is one such polytope for each of the k k message coordinates. Including at most ten inequalities for each affine hull, these contribute O ⁡ ( k ​ q 4 ) O(kq^{4}) public rows. Parity accumulation. The polytope Q ⊕ Q_{\oplus} is the convex hull of four points in ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} and therefore has a constant-size description; there is one for each of the k k steps of the chain, and the endpoint equations p 0 = 0 p_{0}=0 and p k = 0 p_{k}=0 contribute four inequalities. Together these give O ⁡ ( k ) O(k) inequalities, which is absorbed into the last term. With ρ = 8 \rho=8 , one may take a = 56 a=56 , increasing a universal multiplicative constant to cover every family. All descriptions are rational and fixed before the inputs are specified. The conversion in Lemma B.5 adds one homogenizing coordinate and two anchor types; these are counted in Lemma D.3 . Repetitions affect the dataset lengths, but not this count of domain points. ∎ Remark C.4 (Why the parabola) . The embedding e ⁡ ( α j ) = ( j , j 2 ) e(\alpha_{j})=(j,j^{2}) is chosen for three reasons, all visible in Figure 6 . First, a parabola is strictly convex, so no field element lies in the convex hull of the others; had some e ⁡ ( α j ) e(\alpha_{j}) fallen inside, no single inequality could isolate it, and one record could not specify a symbol. Second, the tangent line at e ⁡ ( α j ) e(\alpha_{j}) touches the parabola only there and has integer coefficients, so the pin 2 ​ j ​ z i ( 1 ) − z i ( 2 ) ≥ j 2 2j\,z_{i}^{(1)}-z_{i}^{(2)}\geq j^{2} is rational and uniform in j j ; this matters because every inequality eventually becomes a point of the public data space. Third, two dimensions is the fewest in which q ≥ 3 q\geq 3 points can be in convex position, so the embedding is optimal in the resource that is scarce for us. The alphabet size therefore costs inequalities, never coordinates.

sections.heading: Step 1: construction.
sections.text: Fix an even K ≥ K 0 K\geq K_{0} , where K 0 K_{0} is the universal minimum in Lemma B.2 , increased so that δ ​ K 0 ≥ 2 \delta K_{0}\geq 2 . Let q = 2 s q=2^{s} with s ≥ 1 s\geq 1 . For each such K K , fix once and for all a graph supplied by that lemma. This is a ( 4 , 8 ) (4,8) -biregular graph on K K variable nodes and M = K / 2 M=K/2 check nodes satisfying, for a universal constant δ > 0 \delta>0 , | Γ ⁡ ( T ) | > 2 ​ | T | for every ​ T ⊆ [ K ] ​ with ​ 0 < | T | < δ ​ K , |\Gamma(T)|>2|T|\qquad\text{for every }T\subseteq[K]\text{ with }0<|T|<\delta K, (17) where Γ ⁡ ( a ) ⊆ [ K ] \Gamma(a)\subseteq[K] denotes the support of check a a and Γ ⁡ ( T ) \Gamma(T) the set of checks meeting T T . The same chosen graph is used for every alphabet and every dataset size at this block length. Let H ∈ { 0 , 1 } M × K H\in\{0,1\}^{M\times K} be its incidence matrix, viewed over 𝔽 q \mathbb{F}_{q} , and define 𝒞 H := { c ∈ 𝔽 q K : H c ⊤ = 0 } , k := dim 𝔽 q ( 𝒞 H ) . \displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{H}:=\{c\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{K}:Hc^{\top}=0\},\qquad k:=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}(\mathcal{C}_{H}). Since rank ⁡ ( H ) ≤ M = K / 2 \operatorname{rank}(H)\leq M=K/2 , we have k ≥ K / 2 k\geq K/2 . After relabeling the coordinates, fix a systematic generator G = [ 𝕀 k ∣ A ] ∈ 𝔽 q k × K G=[\mathbb{I}_{k}\mid A]\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k\times K} . Algorithms and Limits for Privately Assessing Data Sharing Mahdi Haghifam Kumar Kshitij Patel Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago Yale University Avrim Blum * Giulia Fanti * Juba Ziani * Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago Carnegie Mellon University Georgia Institute of Technology Abstract In this paper, we study when two parties should pool their data to train a machine learning model. Two agents, Alice and Bob, each hold a sensitive labeled dataset and want to train a classifier from a given hypothesis class ℋ \mathcal{H} . Even when each party’s dataset can be perfectly classified on its own, the two parties may follow conflicting labeling standards or have selection biases that affect their features and label sets, such that no single classifier in ℋ \mathcal{H} fits their combined data. Before committing to data sharing, Alice and Bob therefore want to test whether a single classifier in ℋ \mathcal{H} can jointly fit both datasets—without revealing their individual data points to one another. We formalize this problem from a learning-theoretic viewpoint via opt ℋ \operatorname{opt}_{\mathcal{H}} , the minimum number of mistakes made by any hypothesis in ℋ \mathcal{H} on their pooled data. Through interactive communication, the agents must distinguish opt ℋ = 0 \operatorname{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}=0 (compatible datasets) from opt ℋ ≥ t \operatorname{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}\geq t (conflicting datasets) under pure ε \varepsilon -two-party differential privacy. A trusted curator could do this with t = O ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) t=O(1/\varepsilon) , and we ask how small t t can be without one. For thresholds on the real line over a domain of size m m , we show that the optimal t t is Θ ~ ​ ( log ⁡ log ⁡ m / ε ) 	ilde{\Theta}(\log\log m/\varepsilon) , exponentially smaller than the Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ m / ε ) \Theta(\log m/\varepsilon) samples needed to privately learn thresholds, even with a curator. For halfspaces in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , the dependence on m m jumps to log ⁡ ( m ) \log(m) : we give a protocol with t = O ~ ​ ( d 3 ​ log ⁡ m / ε ) t=	ilde{O}(d^{3}\log m/\varepsilon) and show that some domains require t = Ω ⁡ ( d ​ log ⁡ ( m / d ) / ε ) t=\Omega(d\log(m/d)/\varepsilon) . 0 0 footnotetext: The starred authors are listed in alphabetical order. 0 0 footnotetext: Part of this work was supported by and carried out while Mahdi Haghifam, Giulia Fanti, Kumar Kshitij Patel, and Juba Ziani were visiting the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing. Juba Ziani was supported by NSF awards 2336236 (CAREER) and 2504990. Giulia Fanti was supported in part by NSF award CCF-2338772 (CAREER). 1 Introduction Institutions often hold complementary datasets that capture different aspects of the same downstream learning task. For example, a breast screening clinic may hold primarily negative cases, while a specialized diagnostic center may hold a much higher proportion of confirmed cancer cases [ LASLBKHOTRM17 , SAMHBORLTKLB17 ] . Similarly, organizations trying to detect cybersecurity incidents frequently share data to provide a comprehensive view of the cybersecurity landscape, as attackers may target different organizations with different exploits at different times [ CH23 ] . In such settings, pooling data may enable institutions to learn a useful classifier that no entity could learn on its own. Indeed, this potential was highlighted and analyzed in early theoretical works on distributed machine learning [ BBFM12 ] . Realizing the potential benefit of collaboration, however, often requires institutions to commit resources upfront through legal agreements, financial compensation, governance approvals, and dedicated infrastructure. Before incurring these costs, institutions need to assess the utility of combining their datasets: will pooling improve model accuracy or other downstream metrics enough to justify the collaboration? Yet this assessment depends on joint properties of the datasets, generally hidden from each institution’s local view. Institutions face a circular dilemma: they must judge whether collaboration is worthwhile before committing, yet doing so may require the very data sharing whose value they seek to assess. Privacy requirements further complicate this dilemma. Hospitals, for example, must protect sensitive patient records even when sharing them would help evaluate a collaboration. Institutions may also hesitate to disclose valuable data to a prospective partner who could use them independently and decline to collaborate. When no trusted third party is available, each party must therefore assess whether collaboration is promising while limiting what it reveals about its data. This tension between the need to preserve data privacy while enabling agents to assess the utility of collaboration motivates the main conceptual question of this paper: How can agents estimate whether it is beneficial to combine their datasets while preserving the privacy of individual records? What algorithms can achieve this goal, and what are their fundamental limits? 1.1 How to Assess the Benefits of Data Sharing? In this section, we propose a learning-theoretic notion that agents can use to assess the value of data sharing and provide two real-world scenarios in which it can inform the decision to collaborate. Our focus throughout the paper is on binary classification on a data space (or feature space) 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ d \mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} of size m m for some d ≥ 1 d\geq 1 and a fixed publicly known hypothesis class ℋ ⊆ { ± 1 } 𝒳 \mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{\mathcal{X}} . We consider a setting with two agents, Alice ( A A ) and Bob ( B B ) who respecitvely hold a labeled dataset S A , S B ∈ ( 𝒳 × { ± 1 } ) n S_{A},S_{B}\in(\mathcal{X}	imes\{\pm 1\})^{n} of size n ∈ ℕ n\in\mathbb{N} . We focus on a basic question that arises before joint training: can a single classifier in a given hypothesis class explain both parties’ data? We formalize this question using their joint empirical loss defined as opt ℋ ( S A , S B ) := min h ∈ ℋ ∑ U ∈ { A , B } ∑ ( x , y ) ∈ S U 𝟏 { h ( x ) ≠ y } . \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B}):=
ewmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{U\in\{A,B\}}\sum_{(x,y)\in S_{U}}\mathbf{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{h(x)

(1) We use opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B}) , the number of mistakes made on the pooled data by the best classifier in ℋ \mathcal{H} , to assess the value of combining the data. It is zero when one hypothesis explains both datasets, and large when every hypothesis in ℋ \mathcal{H} makes many mistakes on their union. A large joint loss may indicate conflicting labeling practices, selection biases causing missing features and labels, or that the hypothesis class is not complex enough to fit the combined data. We therefore focus on distinguishing between the following: opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) = 0 \displaystyle\mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})=0 opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) ≥ t \displaystyle\mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})\geq t (2) for some t > 0 t>0 . When opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) = 0 \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})=0 , Alice and Bob agree to collaborate. When opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) ≥ t \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})\geq t , Alice and Bob must reassess 1 1 1 This could take the form of Alice and Bob realizing they do not have the expertise or computing power to fit a good model, in which case they refuse to collaborate; or, this could mean that Alice and Bob need to reconcile their labeling practices, jointly rectify their selection biases to account for missingness, potentially re-label data, or choose a more complex hypothesis class. . Finally, if 0 < opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) < t 0<\mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})<t , we make no claims, as is standard in distribution testing. We now present two examples that further motivate the property-testing problem in ( 2 ). Example 1 (Learning from disparate label sets) . Suppose Alice is a screening clinician and Bob is a diagnostician. They want to develop a classifier to determine whether a patient in a target population should be referred for further diagnostic testing. Their datasets reflect different stages of care: Alice’s screening dataset S A S_{A} mainly contains records of patients who were not referred, whereas Bob’s diagnostic dataset S B S_{B} contains only records of patients who were referred and received more thorough testing [ GBRRDJM11 ] . Since the records contain sensitive patient information, neither agent is willing to disclose individual records to assess a possible collaboration, and no trusted third party is available. To isolate this selection bias, suppose Alice’s labels are all − 1 -1 , and Bob’s are all + 1 +1 . Then, neither can train a useful model alone; they must assess opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B}) to determine whether they can train a low-error model on their joint data. Example 2 (Identifying conflicting labeling practices) . Now suppose Alice has labeled spam and non-spam emails in her dataset. However, her data may be limited or imbalanced, so she wants to augment it with Bob’s curated, labeled email dataset. The challenge is that Bob may have a different view of what constitutes spam, so his labels could conflict with Alice’s data [ KCG24 ] . For example, Alice may label unsolicited promotional emails as spam, while Bob uses that label for fraudulent or malicious messages. Before joint training, Alice wants to know whether a single classifier can achieve a sufficiently low test error under both labeling policies. To isolate conflicting labeling practices, suppose the agents encounter the same distribution of emails but may assign different labels to the same email. In this case, opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) = 0 \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})=0 indicates that, under the hypothesis class H H , Alice’s and Bob’s labeling practices are compatible, implying a collaboration may be worthwhile. On the other end, opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) ≥ t \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})\geq t points to differing labeling practices. Remark 1.1 (From in-sample to in-population error) . Note that our insights extend beyond the in-sample case and hold when considering generalization error over the underlying population distributions. We provide more details using standard arguments in Appendix A . 1.2 Problem Formalization In this section, we formalize our problem and state our main technical question. We first consider the disjoint-label setting as in Example 1 , where Alice holds only negatively labeled examples, and Bob holds only positively labeled ones. Since the labels are fixed by the party holding each record, we suppress them and write S A , S B ∈ 𝒳 n S_{A},\ S_{B}\in\mathcal{X}^{n} . This setting isolates the joint aspect of the problem: when ℋ \mathcal{H} contains the constant predictors, each local dataset is perfectly realizable, but their union need not be. Thus, the local optimal errors alone do not determine whether a common classifier can explain both datasets. For our algorithms, we later show that they extend to datasets with arbitrary label mixtures (see Corollaries 3.13 and 4.8 ). They seek a private assessment algorithm that rejects with high probability when every classifier in ℋ \mathcal{H} makes at least t t mistakes on the pooled data, i.e., opt ℋ ​ ( S A , S B ) ≥ t \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}}(S_{A},S_{B})\geq t . We first explain in Section 1.4.1 the idea behind our lower bound, which is based on the connection between opt ℋ \mathrm{opt}_{\mathcal{H}} and error-correcting codes. We then describe in Section 1.4.2 , our threshold algorithm which uses private binary search over prefix lengths to compare two ordered blocks of data. Finally, in Section 1.4.3 , we explain the ideas behind our algorithm for halfspaces, which is based on the cutting-plane method in the dual space, i.e., classifier space. 1.4.1 Lower Bounds: Coding Against Erasures Our lower bounds use the connection between information complexity and DP [ MMPRTV10 ] . We consider a communication problem in which Alice and Bob receive secrets v A , v B ∈ 𝒱 v_{A},v_{B}\in\mathcal{V} in a finite domain 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , and exchange messages to compute a binary function F : 𝒱 × 𝒱 → { 0 , 1 } F:\mathcal{V}	imes\mathcal{V}	o\{0,1\} .
